name: Positivity offset
statement: At low levels of affective input, positive response is said to exceed negative response, so a neutral or novel situation draws mild approach rather than indifference.
meaning: The offset is one of two asymmetries in Cacioppo and Berntson's evaluative space model. The model treats positivity and negativity as separable activation functions rather than two ends of one scale. The offset is the gap between their intercepts, and the negativity bias is the gap between their slopes. Cacioppo, Gardner and Berntson define the offset as "the tendency for there to be a weak positive (approach) motivational output at zero input". The two asymmetries are not rivals. Both hold at once, at opposite ends of the input range, and the model predicts approach in a bare environment together with a sharper reaction to strong threat. The offset is a parameter recovered from a regression, not a reported mood, and papers that estimate it disagree about which regression to run.

origin.who: John T. Cacioppo, Wendi L. Gardner and Gary G. Berntson
origin.note: The abstract of "Beyond bipolar conceptualizations and measures" names the "positivity offset and negativity bias principles" as the distinct activation functions its review argues for. The model it formalises comes from Cacioppo and Berntson's 1994 Psychological Bulletin review, which Norris and colleagues credit as the source of the model's figure, though this check did not obtain the 1994 text and cannot say whether the phrase appears in it. The fullest statement is the 1999 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology paper, which supplies the definition quoted above.

evidence: The 1999 paper is a theoretical review, and it rests the offset on two studies. One is Gardner's "Biases in impression formation: A demonstration of a bivariate model of evaluation", listed in its reference section as an unpublished doctoral dissertation at Ohio State University. Cacioppo and colleagues report that Gardner found an offset in four studies of impression formation, in judgements of human targets and of novel fish and insects. Searches of the OhioLINK electronic thesis archive, the Ohio State University Libraries catalogue and the open web on 21 September 2026 did not locate that dissertation. The other is Ito, Cacioppo and Lang, who collected positivity and negativity ratings for 472 photographs from the International Affective Picture System. Of it the 1999 paper says "Analyses revealed that the intercept was significantly higher for ratings of positive than for negative stimuli". Norris, Gollan, Berntson and Cacioppo later gathered the supporting literature: spinal extensor responses at low stimulus intensity, mere exposure, mild liking of unknown others, optimistic forecasts, and Harinck and colleagues' finding that gains loom larger than losses for small sums. Their own summary of the state of the field is that "little research has directly examined individual differences in these proposed operating characteristics of the affect system". The individual-differences study they point to, Ito and Cacioppo's 2005 paper, was not read here. Taylor and Francis returned 403 to every request made on 21 September 2026, and Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar both record no open copy. Norris and colleagues describe it as finding the offset normally distributed and stable over about two weeks.

examples.text: Put somebody in an empty room with nothing happening and the reading is not indifference. It is a mild pull towards looking around and touching things, and that pull at zero input is what the offset names.

examples.tag: The fork in an unfamiliar path
examples.text: A walker reaching a fork with nothing known about either route tends to take one rather than turn back. The lean towards going on is small, and it sits where there is nothing in particular to approach or avoid.

examples.tag: The stranger at the next table
examples.text: With nothing said and nothing known, the default towards a stranger is a faint willingness rather than a faint wariness. The same person will react far harder than that to a real threat, and the model expects both at once.

replication.headline: Independent labs recover the offset from arousal ratings, a 261-person German sample putting it at beta = 0.98, while a study of Twitter and Weibo text found the reverse sign.
replication.detail: An independent estimate comes from Riehle, Pillny and Lincoln at Hamburg, who worked from Strauss's clinical adaptation of the model rather than with its authors. Their survey was opened by 521 people, 393 consented, 269 supplied eligible data and 261 remained after long-string responses were dropped. The analysed sample had a mean age of 41.3 years, standard deviation 13.7, range 19 to 75, and rated positivity, negativity and arousal for pleasant, unpleasant and neutral pictures. A multilevel model put the intercept of the positivity activation function at 5.29, 95% CI [4.94, 5.64], and the negativity intercept at 2.89, 95% CI [2.54, 3.24]. The offset, the difference between the two, was a random effect with a mean of 2.40 and a standard deviation of 0.92, beta = 0.98, 95% CI [0.78, 1.18], t(183.2) = 9.64, p < 0.001. The same quantity has been measured four times in clinical work, always as a baseline that illness shrinks. Strauss, Frost, Lee and Gold compared 76 schizophrenia patients with 60 healthy controls. Controls showed the offset, positive intercept 4.7 against negative 3.0, t = 2.33, p < 0.03. Patients ran the other way at a level the paper calls a trend, positive 3.12 against negative 4.2, t = 1.69, p = 0.09. The group difference in the individual offset score was F(1, 134) = 16.68, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.71, patients at M = 1.28, SD = 5.01 and controls at M = 4.98, SD = 5.53. In the same data the controls' negativity bias was not significant, negative slope 0.31 against positive 0.15, t = 1.1, p = 0.26. Bartolomeo, Raugh and Strauss repeated the test in daily life over a week of momentary assessment and geolocation, recruiting 46 patients and 50 controls and analysing 44 and 48 after adherence exclusions. Bartolomeo and colleagues then ran it on people at clinical high risk for psychosis, where 121 high-risk participants and 57 controls completed six days of assessment and 100 high-risk participants met the same adherence rule. Offset scores were 13.49, SD 63.24, against 39.18, SD 23.61, F(1, 156) = 8.69, p = 0.004, eta-squared = 0.05. Their negativity bias difference was not significant, F(1, 156) = 0.43, p = 0.51. Gollan and colleagues compared 41 depressed with 36 healthy participants and put the offset at 0.61, SD 0.55, in controls against 0.30, SD 0.41, in patients, F(1, 75) = 7.69, p = 0.02, eta-squared = 0.09, and the negativity bias at 0.18 against 0.45, F(1, 75) = 5.4, p = 0.02, eta-squared = 0.07. The disagreement comes from outside the laboratory. Cho, Pang, Thapa, Sherman, Ungar, Tay and Guntuku fitted valence and arousal functions to posts from 3,113 US Twitter users, about 3.6 million posts, and to Sina Weibo. They gathered over 29 million Weibo posts from 859,054 people and analysed 668,257 posts from 8,731 of them, scoring text with the NRC-VAD lexicon. They write: "One surprising finding in our study was that we did not find a positivity offset. We instead found a negativity offset for both American and Chinese participants." The intercept gap ran to beta2 = -0.031 on Twitter and -0.016 on Weibo. Their regression predicts arousal from valence, the reverse of the direction Riehle and Strauss use, so the two are not the same test. Yuan, Tian, Huang, Fan and Wei meta-analysed P3 amplitudes, 49 effect sizes from 38 studies and 1,263 subjects, and report that scenic stimuli produce a negativity bias while verbal stimuli produce a positivity offset. Their abstract names arousal, stimulus type and task setting as the significant moderators; cultural background, which they list among the factors examined, is not among them.

study.cite: Riehle, M., Pillny, M., & Lincoln, T. M. (2022). Expanding the positivity offset theory of anhedonia to the psychosis continuum. Schizophrenia, 8, 47.

limits: The name covers at least three quantities. Ito, Cacioppo and Lang regressed unipolar positivity and negativity ratings on rated intensity. Riehle and Strauss regress them on rated arousal and read the offset off the main effect. Cho and colleagues regress arousal on valence and read it off the gap between the two arms of a V. A result in one of these is not a result in the others, and the third is the one that came out with the opposite sign. Cross-cultural coverage is thin. Diener and Diener's 43-nation figure comes from survey life-satisfaction and happiness scales rather than from an activation function, and the German participants in Riehle's study rated pleasant pictures as less arousing than the picture set's US validation sample, Cohen's d = -0.54, which the authors say could indicate a cross-cultural difference. Booy and Carolan ran two experiments on female undergraduates at Simon Fraser University, recruiting 62 for the first and dropping one for low accuracy, and recruiting 71 for the second and retaining 60. Both samples were single-sex and single-site. Searches of Europe PMC, Crossref and the OSF preprint archive on 21 September 2026 found no multi-laboratory or registered replication of the offset itself. Two of the three founding demonstrations were not read here. Gardner's dissertation was not located, and Taylor and Francis refused automated requests for Ito and Cacioppo's 2005 paper. Much of the supporting literature is the same group's, and the four clinical tests that exist were designed to study schizophrenia, psychosis risk and depression, not to check the parameter.
misreadings: The offset is often equated with the finding that most people are happy. Diener and Diener report that in 86% of 43 nations with nationally representative samples the mean subjective wellbeing response was above neutral, and that only India and the Dominican Republic fell below it, on a scale running from 0 to 10. That is a survey mean, and it reaches them through Veenhoven's 1993 summary of almost 1,000 surveys rather than from the surveys themselves. It is consistent with the offset and is not a measurement of it. The second error is reading the offset and the negativity bias as competing claims about whether people lean good or bad. In the model they are the intercept and the slope of one pair of functions, and the negativity bias entry, no. 39, covers the slope. The third is citing the clinical literature as proof that the offset is universal. Strauss, Bartolomeo and Riehle measured it in order to show where it shrinks, and Riehle's data have it falling with negative symptoms, anhedonia, positive symptoms and depression alike. The fourth is treating Gardner's impression-formation studies as published evidence. They are a 1996 dissertation, described in a later review she co-authored.
